title: Batch and async
point: Run work nobody is waiting for through a batch API at roughly half price, and queue expensive work instead of blocking the user.
definition: Batch processing submits many requests together for results within hours, at a discount of roughly half. Asynchronous design queues work and notifies the user later instead of holding a request open.

objective.text: Given a mix of workloads, decide which can move to a batch API or a queue, compute the saving, and state what the user sees while the work waits.

misconceptions.claim: Batching is only for offline data pipelines, not for agent systems.
misconceptions.correction: Agent systems run plenty of work nobody waits for: nightly evaluations, grading, backfills and re-checks. Each can go through a batch API at roughly half price.

misconceptions.claim: Asynchronous means the user gets a worse experience.
misconceptions.correction: A quick acknowledgement and a reliable notification often beat a spinner that times out. Queue the expensive part and show what is ready now.

l1: Ask of each workload whether a person is waiting for it right now. If not, it is a candidate for a batch API, which typically returns results within hours at roughly half price.
Good candidates are overnight grading, evaluation runs, backfills over old documents and periodic re-checks. Interactive chat turns are not.
Async design applies even to user-facing work. Acknowledge the request, queue the expensive part, and notify the user when it completes.
l2: A nightly evaluation runs 5,000 cases at $0.04 each, or $200 a night. Through a batch API at half price it costs $100, so a 30-night month falls from $6,000 to $3,000.
A one-off backfill tags 1 million old documents at $0.01 each. Interactively that is $10,000; through a batch API it is about $5,000, and nobody notices the extra hours.
Neither change affects answer quality. The only cost is waiting, which these workloads can afford.
l3: Split mixed workflows. A contract assistant can return a quick risk summary now and run the full clause-by-clause audit as a batch job, delivered by morning.
Queues also smooth peaks. Work arriving at three times the average rate waits its turn instead of forcing capacity sized for the peak or hitting rate limits.
Discounts may not stack predictably. Cache hits inside a batch can be less reliable, so measure the combined saving rather than multiplying the two headline discounts.
